article_title: Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications
citation: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://www.springer-ny.com
title: ODE method for analyzing stochastic approximation convergence
description: The ODE (ordinary differential equation) method, introduced by Ljung and extensively developed by Kushner and coworkers, is the book's central analytical technique. "The main idea is to show that, asymptotically, the noise eﬀects average out so that the asymptotic behavior is determined eﬀectively by that of a 'mean' ODE." The ODE is obtained by local analysis, averaging the observations as though the parameter were fixed. The authors state that "the ODE method has become a fundamental technique in the current toolbox" and note that constraints, state dependent noise, discontinuities, and other difficulties can be handled, with the ODE replaced by a constrained ODE or differential inclusion as needed.
requirements: Averaging/weak ergodic conditions on the noise processes
Interpolation of the discrete iterates into a continuous time process
constraints: Depending on the application, the ODE might be replaced by a constrained (projected) ODE or a differential inclusion
target_learners: Graduate students and researchers in stochastic optimization and recursive algorithm analysis
target_learning_goals: Proving convergence and rate of convergence of recursive stochastic algorithms under general noise processes and constraints
examples: Convergence proofs for an animal learning example with random step sizes and a pattern classification problem (Chapter 5)
key_sources: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://doi.org/10.1007/b97441

article_title: A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later
citation: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8
title: ODLE framework: multi-agent architecture and component engineering for open distributed learning environments
description: The 1998 paper introduced a framework system for open distributed learning environments combining intelligent support with interactive learning environments. It was, per Fidas et al. as quoted here, characterized by "the combination of intelligent support with interactive learning environments, by the provision of reusable components and by a distributed multi-agent architecture." Openness meant embedding intelligent support into existing face-to-face classrooms and group settings rather than closed-loop private-tutor ITS scenarios, requiring the system to give up full understanding and control of the learning process.
requirements: Intelligent support must be integrated with existing, ecologically valid learning scenarios rather than replacing them
constraints: Openness entails giving up full understanding and control of the learning process on the part of the intelligent system
target_learners: school students in face-to-face classrooms and group learning settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative group learning in mathematics and general problem solving
examples: The approach was exemplified with several applications in mathematics and general problem solving, and applied in EU projects including NIMIS, SEED, COLDEX and Argunaut
key_sources: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8

article_title: Meaningful Biochemistry Learning Using the Orientation-Decision-Do-Discuss-Reflect (OD3R) Method
citation: Yunita Arian Sani Anwar, Senam, & Endang W Laksono. (2018). Meaningful Biochemistry Learning Using the Orientation-Decision-Do-Discuss-Reflect (OD3R) Method. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 17-30. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1132a
title: The OD3R method: a five-stage sequence integrating lecture and laboratory work across cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains
description: The OD3R method is a student-centered instructional method for biochemistry consisting of five stages: orientation to generate motivation, developing/designing the investigation, conducting the investigation, reporting and discussing results, and reflecting on learning. The article states it "consists of 5 stages that integrate learning implementation and laboratory works; integrating assessments on cognitive, affective and psychomotor domains". It was applied to a biochemistry course on qualitative and quantitative analysis of proteins over 2-4 weeks with 2 meetings per week.
requirements: Observers trained to use evaluation instruments assess student activities, with each observer assigned to keep track of 10 students
constraints: The article states that to date there was no method integrating classroom learning and laboratory works in biochemistry learning implementation and assessment in Indonesia, positioning OD3R against cookbook-dominated laboratory practice
target_learners: undergraduate chemistry and chemistry education students
examples: Applied to a biochemistry course on qualitative and quantitative analysis of proteins in 4 state universities in Indonesia, after the same course had been taught conventionally for the carbohydrates topic
key_sources: Yunita Arian Sani Anwar, Senam, & Endang W Laksono. (2018). Meaningful Biochemistry Learning Using the Orientation-Decision-Do-Discuss-Reflect (OD3R) Method. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 17-30. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1132a

article_title: Meaningful Biochemistry Learning Using the Orientation-Decision-Do-Discuss-Reflect (OD3R) Method
citation: Yunita Arian Sani Anwar, Senam, & Endang W Laksono. (2018). Meaningful Biochemistry Learning Using the Orientation-Decision-Do-Discuss-Reflect (OD3R) Method. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 17-30. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1132a
title: Mapping each OD3R stage to learning domains: orientation builds affective motivation, decision trains design, do trains psychomotor skills, discuss develops communication, reflect assesses attitudes
description: The article assigns each OD3R stage a domain profile: orientation generates motivation (affective); decision trains designing group investigations (cognitive and affective); do requires observation, manipulative, drawing, data interpretation, and teaming skills spanning all three domains; discuss develops written reports and presentations across all domains; and review relates to scientific attitudes (affective). Figure 5 presents this mapping as the route to "Meaningful learning in Biochemistry Course".
requirements: Each stage must include its paired activities, e.g. lecturer explanation and group discussion in orientation, individual report writing and lecturer feedback in discuss
constraints: The mapping is the authors' interpretive account of how the stages relate to domains, grounded in Bretz et al.'s criterion that meaningful learning integrates cognitive, affective, and psychomotor aspects
target_learners: undergraduate chemistry and chemistry education students
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning integrating knowledge, skills, and attitudes
examples: In the do stage, students do laboratory work according to their final design and take notes in the form of a temporary report, assessed on observation, drawing, and interpreting skills
key_sources: Yunita Arian Sani Anwar, Senam, & Endang W Laksono. (2018). Meaningful Biochemistry Learning Using the Orientation-Decision-Do-Discuss-Reflect (OD3R) Method. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 17-30. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1132a

article_title: Meaningful Biochemistry Learning Using the Orientation-Decision-Do-Discuss-Reflect (OD3R) Method
citation: Yunita Arian Sani Anwar, Senam, & Endang W Laksono. (2018). Meaningful Biochemistry Learning Using the Orientation-Decision-Do-Discuss-Reflect (OD3R) Method. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 17-30. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1132a
title: Three validated assessment instruments: modified Hoyo rubric for reports, six-type scientific attitude questionnaire, and six-category practical skills rubric
description: The study used three instruments: a modification of the Hoyo rubric (2003) scoring report components (abstracts, information sources, organization, relevance, contents, presentation) on a scale of 1 to 4; a scientific attitudes questionnaire with six attitude types each developed into two indicators with five answer choices; and a practical skills rubric with six categories also scored 1 to 4. The article states the instruments "are validated through expert judgment of 3 experts" and then assessed with 123 respondents, with validity and reliability measured using product moment and alpha cronbach with SPSS 21.
requirements: Instruments must be declared valid and reliable through expert judgment revision and statistical validity and reliability checks before use
constraints: Each assessment component of the report rubric is scored on a scale of 1 to 4 based on the number of criteria students fulfill
examples: The modified Hoyo's rubric, the scientific attitude questionnaire and the practical skills rubric were validated by 3 experts, revised per their advice, and tested on 123 respondents

article_title: Exploring confidence in recognizing oral cancer among dentists and dental students.
citation: Kamran, A., Daniel, Z., Al-Maweri, S. A., Raja, M. (2025). Exploring confidence in recognizing oral cancer among dentists and dental students. Clinical Oral Investigations. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00784-025-06675-w
title: Oral Disease Recognition Scale (ODRS) with seven clinical cases
description: The Oral Disease Recognition Scale is a previously validated instrument containing "seven patient cases encompassing a range of benign, premalignant, and malignant oral conditions", including hairy tongue, leukoplakia, lichen planus, and oral squamous cell carcinoma. Each case presents a brief case history and clinical image with five possible diagnoses; participants select a diagnosis and rate confidence from 1 to 10. In this study it was delivered electronically and used to assess clinicians' oral cancer recognition ability.
requirements: Participants must be shown each case with its case history and clinical image and select from five provided diagnosis options
constraints: The study notes the scale may identify potential cognitive biases but that its findings do not rule out all cognitive bias types
target_learning_goals: Recognition of benign, premalignant, and malignant oral conditions
examples: In this study, 252 dentists and dental students completed the ODRS online, with per-case accuracy ranging from 34.92% (case 7) to 69.84% (case 1)
key_sources: Kamran, A., Daniel, Z., Al-Maweri, S. A., Raja, M. (2025). Exploring confidence in recognizing oral cancer among dentists and dental students. Clinical Oral Investigations. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00784-025-06675-w

article_title: Assessing clinical reasoning in the OSCE: pilot-testing a novel oral debrief exercise.
citation: Régent Alexis, Thampy Harish, Singh Mini. (2023). Assessing clinical reasoning in the OSCE: pilot-testing a novel oral debrief exercise. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04668-5
title: Proposed cognitive model of how clinical reasoning ability is scored during an Oral Debrief
description: The article proposes a cognitive model (Fig. 5) mapping the three think-aloud themes onto the scoring process: candidates' and examiners' own cognitive processes underpin the OD, candidates translate thinking into verbalised responses, and examiners steer discussion through questioning based on their own reasoning. In doing so "the OD elicited comparisons between the candidate's and examiner's illness scripts". The model organises the identified scoring factors, from markers of higher CR ability to markers of poor reasoning, with particular attention to patient safety implications.
requirements: The OD must elicit verbalised reasoning via semi-structured examiner prompts so candidates' thinking can be compared against the examiner's own illness scripts
constraints: The model derives from think-aloud data with sixteen examiners in a small-scale pilot and is offered as a proposed model rather than a validated one
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning assessment in OSCE settings
examples: Think-aloud interviews with sixteen OSCE examiners scoring three scripted OD videos generated the three themes mapped onto the model
key_sources: Régent Alexis, Thampy Harish, Singh Mini. (2023). Assessing clinical reasoning in the OSCE: pilot-testing a novel oral debrief exercise. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04668-5
